headline: High risk of data leakage and cascading errors: CrewAI’s shared-memory orchestration can feed a writable, secret-handling RAG course environment without isolation or verification.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: CrewAI explicitly uses a “subagent_model” with “shared memory” and no default self-isolation, while the course environment exposes writable files and stdin/stdout. That creates a plausible path for attacker-controlled content from agent_b to be treated as instructions by agent_a. The interaction is inferred, not directly documented, so I choose medium over low.
conditions: IF agent_b writes prompt-like content into files or stdout that agent_a later reads as instructions
IF both agents share a host working directory without content provenance checks
mitigations: Separate the agents into different directories
Add a fixed instruction/data delimiter in handoff files
Disable automatic parsing of file contents as prompts
Review any shared-memory handoff before execution
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for inter-agent messages

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both profiles can read and write the host filesystem, and agent_b explicitly handles configuration secrets while agent_a handles API keys for tools and model providers. With agent_a’s broad network egress and no default isolation, sensitive data can flow across the shared workspace and out through model/tool calls. This is a default-dangerous pairwise leakage pathway.
conditions: IF both agents run in the same host workspace
IF either agent reads files containing secrets or configuration tokens
IF agent_a forwards file contents to model providers or tools
mitigations: Put each agent in a separate container or directory
Remove secrets from shared files before either agent runs
Use per-agent environment variables instead of workspace files
Restrict agent_a network egress to approved endpoints
requires-engineering: add secret-scanning and redaction on file reads

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have filesystem write and subprocess execution, so they can race on the same mutable workspace even though neither profile states git writes. CrewAI’s per-process sessions and developer-defined shared state, combined with the course’s local development environment and docker-compose workflow, make overlapping writes plausible. Uncertainty about the exact shared path pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same working directory
IF one agent overwrites notebooks, configs, or generated artifacts used by the other
IF no external lock or job scheduler serializes writes
mitigations: Assign separate output directories
Serialize writes with a simple lock file
Run one agent at a time for shared artifacts
Back up generated files before each run
requires-engineering: add workspace-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: CrewAI’s role-playing crew with shared memory can produce outputs that the course agent may consume in its RAG or agentic-ask flow, and the course exposes multiple API endpoints for downstream actions. If agent_b treats agent_a’s output as authoritative, errors can cascade into incorrect papers, searches, or agentic responses. The lack of a documented verification step makes the safer choice high.
conditions: IF agent_b uses agent_a output as input to /api/v1/ask or /api/v1/agentic-ask
IF no verification or citation-checking step is inserted between agents
IF agent_a emits hallucinated facts or malformed instructions
mitigations: Require a human review step before downstream actions
Add a validation prompt that checks citations and schema
Limit agent_b to read-only summarization of agent_a output
Log and compare outputs against source documents
requires-engineering: implement automated fact verification

E_compliance.rationale: Agent_b explicitly handles configuration secrets and academic/research data in a local development environment, while agent_a handles API keys for tools and model providers. The pair therefore creates a compliance mismatch risk around secret handling and retention, even though no specific residency regime is stated. Because the exact policy gap is undocumented, medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF secrets or research data are stored in shared logs or notebooks
IF retention policies differ between the two environments
IF either agent exports data to third-party services without a DPA
mitigations: Keep secrets out of notebooks and logs
Use separate retention settings for each environment
Mask tokens in console output
Review third-party service terms before use
requires-engineering: document and enforce a data-handling policy
